s: Mrs. Heba, 45, collapses at home two weeks after a long flight. In the ER her pressure is 75/45, her heart rate 130 and her oxygen 84%. A scan shows a large clot in both lung arteries, and the right side of her heart is stretched. She has had no recent surgery, no bleeding and no stroke.
c: A big lung clot with low pressure and a strained right heart, and nothing that makes bleeding likely.

a.w: A clot-busting drug for a big lung clot with low pressure. It dissolves the clot fast.
Fine for a stable clot, but too slow when the pressure is low.
They may help a little, but they don't remove the clot.
It stops new clots reaching the lungs, but doesn't treat the one there now.

lq: What is given for a pulmonary embolism with low blood pressure?

q: What is the small yellow tablet?
s: Mrs. Nermeen, 50, has rheumatoid arthritis, well controlled on a tablet she takes once a week. On a different day each week she also takes a small yellow tablet. Her mouth stays free of ulcers and her blood count is normal. Her friend, on the same weekly drug without the yellow tablet, got painful mouth ulcers and low blood counts.
c: A weekly arthritis drug, plus a tablet on another day that keeps ulcers and low counts away.

a.w: It protects against methotrexate side effects such as mouth ulcers, sickness and low blood counts.
It treats anemia from low iron, not methotrexate side effects.
It protects the bones, not against methotrexate.
It protects the stomach, not against mouth ulcers and low counts from methotrexate.

lq: What is taken with weekly methotrexate to cut its side effects?
la: Folic acid, on a different day

q: What operation did he have?
s: Mr. Magdy, 55, had an operation for a stomach problem a few months ago. Now, about 20 minutes after meals, especially sweet ones, he feels faint and sweaty, with a racing heart, cramps and loose stools. Two hours after eating he sometimes shakes and feels hungry again, with a low sugar. Small meals with less sugar help.
c: After stomach surgery, faintness and cramps soon after sweet meals, then a low sugar two hours later.

a.w: Without the stomach's control, food rushes into the small bowel. Early dumping brings faintness and cramps; late dumping brings a low sugar.
It can cause loose stools after fatty meals, but not faintness and a low sugar.
It doesn't change how food leaves the stomach.
It doesn't touch the stomach or bowel.

lq: Which operation causes dumping syndrome?
la: Stomach surgery, such as a gastrectomy

q: What should be done first?
s: Salma, 6, pulled a cup of hot tea over her arm in the kitchen. The skin is red, with a few blisters starting, over an area about the size of her hand. She is crying but breathing normally, and her clothes on that arm are not stuck to the skin. Her father rushes in from the next room.
t: Cool running water for a burn
c: A scald on a child's arm: the first move is to cool it.

a.w: Cool, not ice-cold, running water for 20 minutes stops the burn going deeper and eases the pain. It helps even up to 3 hours later.
Ice can damage the skin further.
It holds the heat in and raises the risk of infection.
Blisters protect the skin underneath; popping them invites infection.

lq: What is the first aid for a burn?

q: Which tablet is swelling her ankles?
s: Mrs. Samia, 63, was started on a new tablet for high blood pressure six weeks ago, and her readings are now good. Since then both her ankles swell by the evening and leave a dent when pressed. She isn't breathless, she lies flat at night without trouble, and her heart scan, kidney tests and liver tests are normal. The swelling goes down overnight.
c: Both ankles swelling after a new blood pressure tablet, with a normal heart, kidneys and liver.

a.w: Calcium channel blockers widen the small arteries in the legs, so fluid leaks into the ankles. It is a common, harmless side effect.
It can cause cold hands and tiredness, not ankle swelling.
It is known for a dry cough, not swollen ankles.
A water tablet. It would reduce swelling, not cause it.

lq: Which blood pressure tablet commonly causes ankle swelling?
la: Amlodipine and other calcium channel blockers

q: What cleared the itch for the whole family?
s: Ahmed, 12, and his two sisters itch badly at night, mostly between the fingers, around the wrists and around the waist. Their mother itches too. The doctor sees tiny grey lines between the boys' fingers. Everyone in the house put a cream on from neck to toes, left it on overnight, and repeated it a week later. All their bedding was washed hot. The itch slowly went away.
c: A night itch shared by the whole family, tiny lines between the fingers, and a cream from neck to toes repeated after a week.

a.w: It kills the scabies mite. Everyone in the house is treated at the same time, and it is repeated after a week.
It eases itching but doesn't kill the mite, so scabies keeps spreading.
They calm the itch but don't treat the cause.
It treats fungal rashes, which don't leave lines between the fingers or spread through the family this way.

lq: What is the treatment for scabies?
la: Permethrin cream for everyone in the house, repeated after a week

q: What did the doctor do?
s: Mrs. Afaf, 58, gets a few seconds of violent spinning whenever she rolls over in bed or looks up to a high shelf. Her hearing is normal and she has no headache or weakness. When the doctor lays her back quickly with her head turned right, her eyes flicker and she spins. The doctor then moves her head and body through a few set positions, one after another. The spinning stops that day.
c: Short spinning set off by turning in bed, a positive test lying back with the head turned, and a series of head positions.

a.w: A loose crystal in the inner ear canal causes the spinning. Turning the head through set positions moves it back where it belongs.
Sometimes used for Meniere's disease, but they don't move the loose crystal.
They drain fluid from the middle ear and have nothing to do with spinning.
It eases sickness for a short time but doesn't fix the cause.

lq: What is the treatment for benign positional vertigo?

q: What brought her round?
s: Paramedics find Rasha, 24, in a park toilet, hardly breathing. Her lips are blue, she breathes four times a minute, and her pupils are pinpoint. There is a used needle next to her. She is given a spray into her nose. Within two minutes she sits up, breathing well, and wants to leave. The crew warn her it may wear off before the drug does.
c: Pinpoint pupils, very slow breathing, a needle nearby, and a nose spray that works within minutes but may wear off early.

a.w: It reverses opioids within minutes. It wears off faster than many opioids, so patients are watched in case breathing slows again.
It reverses benzodiazepines, which don't cause pinpoint pupils.
It is for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, not opioid overdose.
It treats low sugar, not slow breathing from opioids.

lq: What reverses an opioid overdose?

q: Which diabetes tablet caused this?
s: Mr. Raafat, 70, lives alone and has type 2 diabetes. Two months ago a new tablet was added to his metformin. Twice this week his neighbor found him sweaty, shaking and confused before lunch, and he got better after a sugary drink. His kidney tests are slightly worse than last year. He has also lost his appetite and skips breakfast.
c: A new diabetes tablet, an older man skipping meals, and repeated low-sugar spells.

a.w: It pushes the pancreas to release insulin whatever the sugar level, so it can cause low sugar, especially in older people who skip meals.
On its own it doesn't cause low sugar, and he has taken it for years.
It rarely causes low sugar on its own.
It makes sugar leave in the urine and rarely causes low sugar.

lq: Which diabetes tablets commonly cause low sugar?

q: What treatment clears her confusion?
s: Mrs. Fatma, 64, has cirrhosis. Over two days she has become sleepy and muddled, and she sleeps all day and is awake all night. When she holds her arms out, her hands flap. Her blood ammonia is high. She has been constipated for five days. Her treatment is a sweet syrup three times a day, adjusted until she passes two or three soft stools a day.
c: Cirrhosis, a flapping tremor, a high ammonia after constipation, and a sweet syrup aimed at two to three soft stools a day.

a.w: It draws ammonia out through the bowel and keeps the stools moving, which clears liver confusion.
It slows the bowel, the opposite of what she needs.
A sedative that would make liver confusion much worse.
It lowers stomach acid but does nothing for ammonia.

lq: What is the first treatment for hepatic encephalopathy?

q: What treatment shrank his spleen?
s: Mr. Sherif, 30, has had easy bruising, bone pain and a big belly since his teens. His spleen and liver are very large, and his platelets are low. A blood test shows a missing enzyme, and a gene test confirms an inherited storage disease. He now has a drip every two weeks for life. After a year his spleen is smaller and his platelets are up.
c: An inherited storage disease, a missing enzyme, and a drip every two weeks for life.

a.w: In Gaucher disease the missing enzyme is given back by drip, so stored fat clears from the spleen, liver and bones.
It removes the big spleen but leaves the fat building up in the bones and liver.
Rarely used, with high risk, and it isn't a drip every two weeks.
They don't replace the missing enzyme.

lq: What is the main treatment for Gaucher disease?

q: Which new tablet caused this?
s: Nesma, 29, was found to have low iron after heavy periods and started a tablet twice a day. Within days her stools turned black and she became constipated, with a little stomach ache. She has no vomiting of blood, no dizziness, and her pressure and pulse are normal. Her hemoglobin is already rising.
c: Low iron, a new twice-daily tablet, then black stools and constipation with a rising hemoglobin.

a.w: Iron tablets often turn the stools black and cause constipation and stomach upset. This is harmless.
It doesn't turn the stools black.
It reduces heavy periods, but doesn't blacken the stools.
It doesn't cause black stools or constipation.

lq: What harmless change do iron tablets cause in the stools?

q: Which TB drug stopped her pill working?
s: Mai, 23, started four tablets for tuberculosis last month. Her urine and tears turned orange-red, as her doctor warned. She has taken her contraceptive pill every day without missing one. Today her pregnancy test is positive. She takes no other medicines, and her liver tests are normal.
c: Four TB tablets, orange urine and tears, and a contraceptive pill that failed without a missed dose.

a.w: It speeds up how the liver breaks down hormones, so the pill stops working. It also turns body fluids orange-red.
It can cause nerve damage, prevented with vitamin B6, but it doesn't stop the pill working.
It can cause gout and liver damage, not pill failure.
It can harm eyesight, not the pill.

lq: Which TB drug makes the contraceptive pill fail?

q: What treatment did he have?
s: Mr. Hesham, 44, had bad pain in his side from a kidney stone, 12 mm across, that wasn't passing by itself. He lay on a table while a machine outside his body sent shock waves at the stone for about an hour. No cut was made and no camera went inside. Over the next week his urine looked gritty and slightly pink, and he passed small pieces of stone.
c: A stone too big to pass, shock waves from outside the body, no cut and no camera, then gritty urine.

a.w: Shock waves break the stone into small pieces that pass in the urine over the next days.
A camera goes up the urine tube to break or remove the stone, but no camera went in.
It needs a cut, and is rarely done now.
A tablet that relaxes the urine tube to help small stones pass. It isn't a machine.

lq: How can a kidney stone be broken without a cut or a camera?

q: What daily tablet cut her migraines?
s: Rasha, 34, had migraines with flashing lights eight times a month, and painkillers no longer kept up. Her doctor started a daily tablet to prevent them. Over three months her attacks dropped to two a month. She noticed her hands are colder and her pulse is slower. She has no asthma, and her pressure is normal-low.
c: A daily tablet that cut migraines, with cold hands and a slow pulse.

a.w: A beta-blocker that prevents migraines. Cold hands and a slower pulse are its usual side effects.
It treats an attack once it starts but isn't a daily preventer.
It eases the pain of an attack and doesn't prevent migraines.
It can cause rebound headaches and doesn't prevent migraines.

lq: Which daily tablet is a common migraine preventer?

q: Which epilepsy tablet should have been changed before pregnancy?
s: Nada, 26, has had epilepsy since her teens and takes the same tablet twice a day, which controls her fits well. She didn't plan this pregnancy. At her 20-week scan, the baby's lower spine is open. Her doctor says the tablet carries the highest risk of birth defects and lower IQ of all the epilepsy drugs, and should have been switched beforehand.
c: An epilepsy tablet with the highest risk of spine defects and lower IQ in the baby.

a.w: It carries the highest risk of spina bifida and learning problems in the baby, so women who could get pregnant should be switched.
One of the safest epilepsy drugs in pregnancy.
Also one of the safest choices in pregnancy.
It lowers the risk of spine defects. It doesn't cause them.

lq: Which epilepsy drug is avoided in women who could get pregnant?

q: Which long-term tablet damaged her retina?
s: Mrs. Hanaa, 58, has had lupus for 12 years and has taken the same daily tablet all along. She never went to her yearly eye checks. Now she finds it hard to read, with gaps in the middle of words. The eye doctor sees a ring-shaped "bull's eye" pattern around the center of each retina. Her lupus is calm.
c: Twelve years of a lupus tablet, missed yearly eye checks, and a bull's eye pattern on the retina.

a.w: Over many years it can damage the retina in a bull's eye pattern, which is why yearly eye checks are needed.
Long use can cause cataracts and glaucoma, not a bull's eye retina.
It affects the liver and blood count, not the retina.
It affects the blood count and liver, not the retina.

lq: Which drug needs yearly eye checks because of retina damage?

q: What helped his numb fingers at night?
s: Mr. Ehab, 41, a typist, wakes at night with tingling in his thumb, index and middle fingers, which he shakes to get rid of. Tapping the inside of his wrist sends tingles into those fingers. His little finger is fine, and the muscle at the base of his thumb is not wasted. He wore something on his wrist every night for six weeks, and the tingling settled.
c: Night tingling in the first three fingers, a positive wrist tap, no wasting, and something worn at night.

a.w: Holding the wrist straight at night takes pressure off the median nerve and settles mild carpal tunnel syndrome.
Used when splints and injections fail, or when the thumb muscle wastes.
It protects the ulnar nerve, which supplies the little finger, not these fingers.
They treat nerve damage from low B12, which affects both feet and hands, not three fingers.

lq: What is the first treatment for mild carpal tunnel syndrome?

q: What is the antidote in the drip?
s: Malak, 3, swallowed most of her mother's pregnancy tablets an hour ago. She vomited twice, with some blood, and has belly pain and diarrhea. An X-ray shows many small white tablets in her stomach. Her blood level of the tablet's metal is very high. A drip is started that turns her urine a red-orange color.
c: A toddler who swallowed pregnancy tablets, tablets seen on X-ray, and a drip that turns the urine red-orange.

a.w: It binds iron in the blood so it leaves in the urine, which turns a red-orange "vin rosé" color.
It doesn't bind iron, so it doesn't help here.
It is the antidote for paracetamol, not iron.
It reverses warfarin, not iron.

lq: What is the antidote for iron poisoning?

q: Which tablet did the tramadol react with?
s: Mr. Wagih, 38, has taken a daily tablet for depression for a year. After a back injury, he was given tramadol. Two days later he is agitated and sweating, with a temperature of 38.6, a fast heart, dilated pupils and diarrhea. His legs twitch and jerk, more than his arms, and his knee reflexes are very brisk. He takes no illegal drugs.
c: A daily depression tablet, new tramadol, then agitation, fever, sweating and jerking legs with brisk reflexes.

a.w: Together with tramadol it raises serotonin too much: serotonin syndrome, with fever, agitation and jerking, mostly in the legs.
With other drugs it can cause stiffness and fever, but not jerking legs and brisk reflexes.
It is a mood stabilizer, not a daily depression tablet here, and tramadol doesn't push it up.
It would calm him, not cause this.

lq: Which painkiller can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs?

q: Which inhaler caused the white patches?
s: Mr. Gamal, 52, has asthma and was started on a new inhaler twice a day, which keeps him well. Two months later he has white patches inside his mouth that rub off and leave red spots, and his voice is hoarse. He doesn't rinse his mouth after using it and doesn't use a spacer. He uses his blue reliever only now and then.
c: A daily preventer inhaler, no rinsing, then white patches in the mouth and a hoarse voice.

a.w: Steroid inhalers can cause mouth thrush and a hoarse voice. A spacer and rinsing the mouth prevent it.
The blue reliever can cause a tremor and fast heart, not thrush.
It can cause a dry mouth, but not thrush like this.
They can cause bad dreams and mood changes, not thrush.

lq: How is thrush from steroid inhalers prevented?
la: Use a spacer and rinse the mouth after each dose

q: What tablet treated his gout attack?
s: Mr. Salem, 60, woke with a red, hot, swollen big toe that he couldn't bear the bedsheet touching. He has kidney disease, so his doctor avoided ibuprofen. He was given small tablets two or three times a day for a few days, and the pain eased. He was told to stop them at once if he got diarrhea. On the third day loose stools began, and he stopped.
c: A gout attack with kidney disease, so no ibuprofen, and small tablets to stop if diarrhea starts.

a.w: It calms a gout attack when NSAIDs aren't safe. Diarrhea is the sign to stop it.
It prevents future attacks but isn't started to treat one.
It works for gout, but the doctor avoided it because of his kidneys.
Like allopurinol, it lowers uric acid over time rather than treating the attack.

lq: Which gout attack drug is stopped if diarrhea starts?

q: Which drug should have been stopped before the operation?
s: Mr. Hamed, 68, has an artificial heart valve and takes a daily blood thinner, checked by INR. He was booked for a hernia repair. Nobody looked at his tablets before surgery, and his INR on the morning of the operation was 3.4. The wound bled for hours afterwards and he needed blood. His platelets are normal.
c: A metal heart valve, a thinner checked by INR, and an INR of 3.4 on the day of surgery.

a.w: It is stopped about five days before planned surgery. With a metal valve, heparin covers the gap.
It is often continued for small operations, and it doesn't raise the INR.
It is continued and doesn't cause bleeding.
It is continued before surgery and doesn't cause bleeding.

lq: How long before planned surgery is warfarin usually stopped?
la: About five days, with bridging heparin if the clot risk is high

q: What should be given straight away?
s: At a restaurant, Karim, 15, eats a dessert that had nuts in it, although he is allergic. Within minutes his lips swell, he has hives on his neck, his voice is hoarse and he is wheezing. He feels faint. In his school bag is the pen his doctor gave him. His friend has already called an ambulance.
c: A known nut allergy, swelling, wheeze and faintness within minutes, and a pen from his doctor.

a.w: Adrenaline is the first treatment for anaphylaxis. It is given into the outer thigh, even through clothes, and repeated after 5 minutes if needed.
It helps hives but is too slow and too weak for anaphylaxis.
It may ease wheeze a little, but it doesn't stop the swelling or fainting.

a.o: Sit him up and wait for the ambulance
a.w: Waiting loses time. Adrenaline comes first, and a faint person lies with legs raised.

lq: What is the first treatment for anaphylaxis?

q: Which heart tablet has built up too high?
s: Mrs. Zeinab, 81, has an irregular heartbeat and a weak heart. She has taken the same small heart tablet for years. After a bout of vomiting and diarrhea, her kidney tests have worsened. Now she feels sick, sees yellow-green rings around lights, and is confused. Her pulse is 44 and her potassium is low. Her ECG shows a "reverse tick" shape.
c: Yellow-green vision, sickness, a slow pulse and a reverse tick on the ECG after the kidneys worsened.

a.w: It is cleared by the kidneys, so it builds up when they fail. Yellow vision, sickness and a slow pulse are classic, worse with low potassium.
It slows the pulse but doesn't cause yellow vision or the reverse tick.
It can harm the thyroid, lungs and eyes, but not with yellow rings like this.
It thins the blood; too much causes bleeding, not these signs.

lq: Which heart drug causes yellow-green vision when its level is too high?

q: What was stopped that made her psoriasis explode?
s: Mrs. Lamia, 47, has had mild plaque psoriasis for years. A month ago, for a bad chest, she was given a short course of strong tablets, and her skin cleared beautifully. She stopped them at the end of the week as told. Ten days later she is covered in widespread small pus spots on red skin, with a fever. She has never had this before.
c: Psoriasis that cleared on a short course of tablets for the chest, then pus spots everywhere days after they stopped.

a.w: Stopping steroid tablets in psoriasis can trigger a severe flare with pus spots. Steroid tablets are avoided in psoriasis.
It can cause a rash, but not a pustular psoriasis flare after stopping.
Stopping it doesn't affect the skin.
It doesn't affect psoriasis.

lq: Why are steroid tablets avoided in psoriasis?
la: Stopping them can trigger a severe pustular flare

q: Which treatment in hospital damaged her hearing?
s: Mrs. Basma, 62, had a severe kidney infection six weeks ago and spent ten days in hospital on drips. Her kidney numbers rose while she was there, and no one checked her drug levels. Since going home she has ringing in both ears, she can't hear high voices, and she feels unsteady walking in the dark. Her ears look normal.
c: Ten days of drips for a kidney infection, unchecked drug levels, then ringing, high-tone deafness and poor balance.

a.w: It can damage the inner ear and balance, especially when levels aren't checked and the kidneys worsen. The damage is often permanent.
It doesn't harm hearing.
It doesn't damage the inner ear.
Fluids don't harm hearing.

lq: Which antibiotic group can damage hearing and balance?

q: Which tablets did he take?
s: Mr. Ayman, 35, took a large number of tablets six hours ago. He now has ringing in his ears, he is sweating, vomiting and breathing deep and fast. His temperature is 38. His first blood gas showed a low CO2, and now it shows acid in the blood as well. He is given a drip of bicarbonate to make his urine alkaline.
c: Ringing ears, fast breathing, a blood gas going from low CO2 to acid, and alkaline urine as treatment.

a.w: Aspirin overdose first drives fast breathing, then acid builds up. Making the urine alkaline helps clear it.
It looks harmless at first and harms the liver, without ringing ears or this blood gas.
Overdose usually causes stomach upset and, rarely, kidney problems, not ringing ears.
Overdose causes drowsiness, fits and a wide QRS. Bicarbonate is used for the heart, not the urine.

lq: What overdose causes ringing in the ears and fast breathing?

q: Which thyroid tablet is preferred in early pregnancy?
s: Sara, 29, has an overactive thyroid that was controlled on a tablet for a year. She has just found out she is six weeks pregnant. Her doctor switches her to another thyroid tablet for the first three months, because her usual one can cause rare scalp and gut defects in the baby. Later in the pregnancy she may switch back.
c: An overactive thyroid in the first three months of pregnancy, and a switch away from the usual tablet.

a.w: It is preferred in the first three months, because carbimazole can cause rare birth defects then.
Her usual tablet, which is avoided in the first three months.
It treats an underactive thyroid, the opposite problem.
It is never given in pregnancy, as it destroys the baby's thyroid.

lq: Which thyroid drug is preferred in the first three months of pregnancy?

q: Which treatment didn't clear his ulcer for good?
s: Mr. Raed, 45, had burning upper belly pain at night, eased by food. A camera showed a duodenal ulcer, and a breath test was positive for a germ. He took a tablet to lower acid for two months and felt fine. Three months after stopping, the pain is back and the breath test is still positive. He doesn't take painkillers.
c: A positive germ breath test that stayed positive after two months of an acid tablet alone.

a.w: It lowers acid and heals the ulcer, but without antibiotics the germ stays and the ulcer comes back.
A PPI with two antibiotics clears the germ. He never had it.
He didn't take it, and it only eases symptoms for a short time.
Not needed for most ulcers once the germ is cleared.

lq: What clears H. pylori?
la: A PPI with two antibiotics (triple therapy)

q: What lowered the risk for her second baby?
s: Mrs. Asmaa, 30, had a first baby born with an open spine. Before trying again, her doctor told her to start a high-dose tablet three months before getting pregnant and to keep taking it for the first three months. Her second baby is born with a normal spine. Her cousin, who did not take it, had a baby with the same problem.
c: A first baby with an open spine, and a high-dose tablet started months before the next pregnancy.

a.w: 5 mg a day before and in early pregnancy cuts the risk of spine defects, especially after an affected baby.
They prevent anemia, not spine defects.
High doses can harm the baby.
It helps the bones, not the spine closing.

lq: What dose of folic acid is used after a baby with a neural tube defect?
la: 5 mg a day, before and in early pregnancy

q: What daily tablet cut her pain crises?
s: Hagar, 16, has sickle cell disease and used to be admitted with pain crises every month. Two years ago she started a daily capsule, with blood counts checked often. Since then she has had only two crises and no chest crisis. Her red cells are bigger than before, and her blood shows more baby-type hemoglobin.
c: A daily capsule in sickle cell disease, bigger red cells, and more baby-type hemoglobin.

a.w: It raises fetal hemoglobin, which stops cells sickling, so crises and chest crises fall. Blood counts are checked for low white cells.
It is given in sickle cell, but it doesn't raise fetal hemoglobin or cut crises.
Not given unless iron is low, and they don't prevent crises.
It prevents infections in children with sickle cell, not pain crises.

lq: Which daily drug raises fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease?

q: Which treatment did he stop too early?
s: Mr. Yasser, 39, was diagnosed with tuberculosis four months ago and felt much better after six weeks of tablets. Feeling well, he stopped them. Now his cough and night sweats are back, and his sputum grows the germ again. This time, lab tests show it no longer responds to the two main drugs he took.
c: TB tablets stopped early once he felt well, and the germ coming back resistant.

a.w: TB needs at least six months. Stopping early lets the germ come back and become resistant.
Stopping it doesn't bring back TB.
It prevents nerve damage from isoniazid. Stopping it doesn't cause resistance.
It only eases the cough.

lq: Why must the full six-month TB course be finished?
la: Stopping early lets TB come back and become resistant

q: Which water tablet set off his gout?
s: Mr. Atef, 66, has a weak heart and was started on a strong water tablet in the morning, which eased his breathlessness and swollen legs. Two weeks later his big toe is red, hot and swollen overnight, and he can't stand the bedsheet on it. His uric acid is high. He drinks little alcohol and hasn't changed his diet.
c: A new strong water tablet, then a hot, swollen big toe and a high uric acid.

a.w: Loop and thiazide water tablets raise uric acid, which can trigger gout.
It can raise potassium and cause breast swelling, but it doesn't usually cause gout.
It causes cough and high potassium, not gout.
It doesn't raise uric acid.

lq: Which drugs can trigger gout by raising uric acid?
la: Water tablets, such as furosemide and thiazides

q: Which epilepsy tablet is too high?
s: Mr. Fouad, 33, has epilepsy. Last month his dose was raised a little after a fit. Now he walks like he is drunk, his speech is slurred, and his eyes flicker side to side when he looks left or right. He hasn't been drinking. His gums have grown thick over his teeth over the years. The drug level comes back high.
c: A small dose rise, then an unsteady walk, slurred speech and flickering eyes, with thick gums over the years.

a.w: A small dose rise can push its level up a lot. Too much causes unsteadiness and flickering eyes; long use thickens the gums.
It can affect mood, but doesn't cause thick gums or rise sharply with small dose changes.
It can cause a serious rash, not thick gums.
It can cause tremor and weight gain, not thick gums.

lq: Which epilepsy drug thickens the gums?

q: Which treatment failed?
s: Lobna, 22, takes a pill for contraception that has only one hormone, every day with no break. Last month she started a new job with night shifts, and twice she took it about 5 hours late. She didn't use condoms afterwards. Today her pregnancy test is positive. She takes no other medicines.
c: A one-hormone pill taken with no break, twice taken hours late.

a.w: The traditional one must be taken within 3 hours of the usual time, or it may fail.
It has two hormones and a 12-hour window, and it usually has a break.
It isn't a pill and doesn't depend on timing.
It sits under the skin and doesn't depend on daily timing.

lq: How late can a traditional progestogen-only pill be taken?

q: What treatment did he stop?
s: Mr. Hossam, 70, was told years ago that the pressure in his eyes was high and was given drops each night. He stopped them a year ago because his sight seemed fine and the drops stung. Now he keeps bumping into doorframes on his left side. His eye pressure is high and his side vision has shrunk to a tunnel.
c: High eye pressure treated with nightly drops, stopped because sight seemed fine, then tunnel vision.

a.w: Glaucoma steals side vision without symptoms. Stopping the drops lets the pressure rise and the damage is permanent.
They ease dry eyes. Stopping them doesn't cause tunnel vision.
They treat infections and don't control pressure.
They can raise eye pressure, not lower it.

lq: Why must glaucoma drops be used even without symptoms?
la: Glaucoma damages side vision silently and the loss is permanent

q: What operation did she have?
s: Mrs. Kawthar, 72, had an operation six weeks ago after years of hip pain. Today she bent low to pick up her slipper while sitting on a soft sofa and felt a clunk. Her leg is now short and turned in. An X-ray shows the metal ball has come out of its plastic cup. She was told after surgery not to bend her hip past a right angle.
c: A metal ball out of its plastic cup after bending low, weeks after an operation for hip pain.

a.w: In the first weeks it can dislocate if the hip bends too far, which is why patients avoid low seats and bending deep.
A keyhole operation that leaves no metal ball.
Screws hold a broken neck of the femur; there is no ball and cup.
The wrong joint.

lq: What movement is avoided early after a hip replacement?
la: Bending the hip past a right angle (low seats, deep bending)

q: Why did her inhaler not work?
s: Sondos, 6, has asthma and wakes coughing at night. She has a preventer inhaler twice a day, but nothing improves. At the clinic she shows how she uses it: she presses it straight into her mouth while breathing out, and most of the mist hits her cheek. She has never used the plastic tube that came with it.
c: A child pressing the inhaler while breathing out, mist on her cheek, and an unused plastic tube.

a.w: Young children can't time the puff with a breath. A spacer holds the mist so it reaches the lungs.
She doesn't take it, and her problem is technique, not the drug.
Not needed if the preventer reaches her lungs.
Asthma isn't an infection.

lq: What helps children get inhaler medicine into the lungs?

q: Which tablet did she stop suddenly?
s: Mrs. Rehab, 41, took a daily tablet for anxiety and depression for two years. She felt better and stopped it all at once. Three days later she feels dizzy, has "electric shock" feelings in her head when she moves her eyes, feels sick, irritable and has vivid dreams. She has no fever and her bloods are normal.
c: Brain-zaps, dizziness and vivid dreams days after a daily anxiety tablet was stopped at once.

a.w: SSRIs with a short life, especially paroxetine, cause withdrawal when stopped suddenly. They are stopped slowly.
It lasts long in the body, so stopping it rarely causes withdrawal.
Stopping it risks a relapse of mania, not brain-zaps.
Stopping it suddenly can cause fits and shakes, not mainly brain-zaps.

lq: Which SSRI causes the worst withdrawal when stopped suddenly?

q: Which tablet damaged his lungs?
s: Mr. Sabry, 70, has had an irregular heartbeat for two years, controlled on a daily tablet. His skin turns blue-grey in the sun, and last year his thyroid became underactive. Now he is short of breath on walking, with a dry cough. His CT shows scarring in both lungs. He never smoked and never worked with dust.
c: A heart rhythm tablet, blue-grey skin, thyroid trouble, and lung scarring.

a.w: Long use can scar the lungs, upset the thyroid and turn the skin blue-grey.
It can worsen asthma but doesn't scar the lungs.
It doesn't scar the lungs or upset the thyroid.
It doesn't affect the lungs this way.

lq: Which heart rhythm drug can scar the lungs and upset the thyroid?

q: Which tablet should not have been given with her methotrexate?
s: Mrs. Fawzia, 63, has rheumatoid arthritis on weekly methotrexate. She went to a walk-in clinic with a urine infection and was given an antibiotic twice a day for a week. Now she has mouth ulcers, a fever and bruises, and her blood count is very low. She took the methotrexate correctly, once a week.
c: Weekly methotrexate, a new antibiotic for a urine infection, then a crashed blood count.

a.w: It also blocks folate, so with methotrexate it can wipe out the bone marrow. The two are not given together.
A safer choice for a urine infection with methotrexate.
It doesn't block folate like trimethoprim.
It is safe with methotrexate.

lq: Which antibiotic is dangerous with methotrexate?

q: What was missed that let her lungs fill?
s: Mrs. Nawal, 70, had bowel surgery two days ago. Her belly is swollen and silent, and she is vomiting green fluid again and again. Overnight, while lying flat, she breathed some vomit into her lungs and now has a fever and crackles on the right. The nurses had kept her eating soup and had not put any tube in.
c: A swollen, silent belly after surgery with green vomiting, food continued, and no tube.

a.o: Nasogastric tube with nil by mouth
a.w: In a stopped bowel, a tube through the nose drains the stomach and stops vomiting that can go into the lungs.
They don't help a stopped bowel and can make vomiting worse.
It doesn't empty the stomach.
It helps the bowel restart, but doesn't stop vomiting now.

lq: What is the first step in a stopped bowel after surgery with vomiting?
la: Nil by mouth and a nasogastric tube to drain the stomach

q: What should be done while waiting for the ambulance?
s: A man in his 40s collapses at a bus stop. He doesn't answer when spoken to or gently shaken, but he is breathing normally, his chest rising and falling. There is no sign of a neck injury and he didn't fall from a height. A passer-by has called an ambulance and is still on the phone.
c: Unresponsive but breathing normally, with no sign of a neck injury.

a.w: Rolling him onto his side keeps the airway open and lets any vomit drain. Keep checking his breathing.
CPR is only for someone not breathing normally.
Never give anything by mouth to an unresponsive person.

a.o: Sit him up against the wall
a.w: He may slump and block his airway.

lq: What is done for someone unresponsive but breathing normally?
la: Place them in the recovery position and keep checking breathing
